Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recording ID: fireflies-20270411-axiom-001-bk7

Summary (auto):
Customer evaluates Redwood for low-latency streaming inference for conversational routing and telematics summarization. Primary concerns: p95 token latency targets during streaming, sustained concurrency during morning peaks, data residency and private deployment for PII in logs. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs and benchmarking plan.

Topics:
- p95 streaming token latency targets
- concurrency & burst sizing
- token/sec throughput and batching tradeoffs
- KV cache and cold-start impacts
- security/SOC2 & VPC option for logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Ramos: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Marcus Li: Hey Alex, good thanks. A busy day but ready to dig in.
[00:09] Jenna Ortiz: Hi all. I'm Jenna, we'll probably ask a lot about network egress and how logs are handled.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Great, Jenna. We'll cover both infra and security. I'm Priya, I'll take the technical parts.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir here, ML eng, I own the prompt infra and model experiments. We have a couple of real-world prompt shapes to run.
[00:25] Alex Ramos: Awesome. Quick agenda: we want to understand your p95 goals for streaming, concurrency needs, and then map Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private options and next steps.
[00:35] Marcus Li: High level — our app is voice -> transcription -> LLM streaming for intent detection and short summary sent back to driver. We have two windows: morning surge 07:00-09:00 and evening 17:00-19:00. Peak concurrency around 120-180 streams concurrently, average session 30s but we stream tokens continuously. P95 latency target is tough: we want token-to-token latency under 80ms p95 ideally, 150ms max.
[00:59] Priya Nair: 80ms p95 token latency is ambitious for streaming; depends on model size, sequence length, and whether you use hosted low-latency variants or dedicated GPU pools. For context, our smallest low-latency variants on hosted can hit ~60-120ms p95 for small-medium LMs at 512 token context when optimized. Larger 13B+ tends to be higher unless you pin dedicated capacity and tune batch sizes.
[01:24] Jenna Ortiz: When you say "pin dedicated capacity", do you mean reserved GPUs that always run our model? What are the failure modes when load spikes?
[01:32] Priya Nair: Yes. Dedicated means you get reserved workers — consistent KV cache residency and predictable per-token compute. During spikes, we offer burst capacity (optional) that can spin up additional instances but with some cold-start penalty. Hosted has autoscaling, but during a huge spike you may see brief increases in p95 as requests get routed to warm-up workers or smaller quantized variants as fallback.
[01:52] Marcus Li: Could you ballpark throughput? If we have 150 concurrent streams and each produces say 10 tokens/sec on average, that's 1500 tokens/sec sustained. What GPU profile do we need?
[02:03] Priya Nair: Roughly, if you're using a 7B model with optimized kernels and 4-bit quant, a single A100 (or equivalent) in our Dedicated pool can sustain ~2k-3k tokens/sec for autoregressive workloads with moderate batching. For 13B it's lower, maybe 1k-1.5k tokens/sec. The streaming token-to-token latency is influenced by micro-batching windows — we can configure a small continuous batching window to keep per-token latency low.
[02:32] Alex Ramos: Also consider prefix caching and KV cache warmness: if many sessions reuse similar prompts (like standard instruction + small user context), caching reduces work. If every session is unique, your token/sec demands increase.
[02:46] Samir Patel: Our prompts are mostly templated with a few driver-specific fields — so there is some prefix reuse. We also do short summaries every 10-15s which adds extra tokens. So maybe 12 tokens/sec average.
[02:58] Jenna Ortiz: On private deployment: we have regulatory constraints around PII in telematics logs — would Redwood Private let us keep logs on-prem and only use control plane? How does billing work?
[03:10] Priya Nair: Private allows control plane to be customer-managed; you can configure local log sinks and HSM/KMS integrations. Billing typically is enterprise license + infra. We can also run a hybrid where model inference runs in your VPC (private) while Redwood manages orchestration.
[03:25] Marcus Li: That sounds promising. Cost-wise for Dedicated vs Hosted, do you have numbers for our expected sustained 1.5k-2k tokens/sec?
[03:33] Alex Ramos: I'll share a detailed cost matrix after this call, but high-level: Hosted per-token is simplest for eval — but for sustained high throughput Dedicated reserved capacity often becomes cheaper and more predictable. For 24/7 sustained load, Dedicated with reserved commits usually wins. We can run a cost proforma tailored to your prompt shape.
[03:50] Speaker 1: (unintelligible)
[03:53] Priya Nair: One planning detail — p95 token latency target of 80ms means we should optimize for micro-batch size of 1-2 tokens and tune kernel paths; that increases per-token overhead but keeps latency tight. There's a cost tradeoff: smaller batches reduce throughput efficiency.
[04:12] Samir Patel: If we accept 150ms p95, does that change hardware needs?
[04:16] Priya Nair: Yes, 150ms p95 is more forgiving — you can allow slightly larger micro-batches and higher accelerator utilization, needing fewer GPUs. We'll model both SLO bands in the benchmark.
[04:27] Marcus Li: Any notes on tokenization or tokenizer overhead? Our voice pipeline emits subword tokens — we saw in prior infra tests tokenizer can add 10-30ms at scale.
[04:35] Priya Nair: Good callout. Redwood can host the tokenizer close to the model execution path; in Dedicated setups we can colocate tokenizer service on the same node to reduce RTT. We'll include tokenizer profiling in the benchmark script.
[04:47] Jenna Ortiz: Network egress — during peak we saw spikes in RTOs when egress limits were hit. For hosted, how do you guarantee throughput to regions?
[04:56] Alex Ramos: We have regional endpoints. For strict egress and residency controls, Private with VPC peering is recommended. For Hosted we can prioritize routes by region and fall back across adjacent regions, but that's subject to cloud bandwidth limits. We'll surface documented throughput baselines per region in the follow-up.
[05:14] Marcus Li: What about fallback policy — say one model variant is overloaded, can Redwood route to a smaller quantized model automatically?
[05:20] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing supports fallback chains by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or custom. For latency SLOs you'd pick latency-first and the system will fallback to a compatible model variant with a similar API. You can control fallback order.
[05:33] Samir Patel: For benchmarking, we'd want to replay a 1-hour morning surge with real traffic. Can Redwood replay traffic into Dedicated test workers?
[05:41] Priya Nair: Absolutely. We have a benchmark harness that replays traffic, records per-token latency (p50/p95/p99), concurrency profiles, and token/sec. We'll run an initial smoke test on Hosted for quick intel, then a Dedicated run with pinned capacity to validate steady-state.
[05:56] Alex Ramos: Priya, maybe outline the benchmark steps?
[05:58] Priya Nair: Sure. Step 1: ingest the prompt set and traffic profile from Axiom. Step 2: smoke run on Hosted low-latency to validate functional correctness and gather baseline. Step 3: Dedicated run with configs: micro-batch window 10-15ms, KV cache warm-up period 10 minutes, quantization Q4_optimized for 7B or Q8 for 13B. Step 4: measure p95 token latency, tail latency, and cost per 1k tokens; run several scenarios: 120 concurrent, 180 concurrent, and 240 burst. We'll also measure cold-start behavior and burst ramp.
[06:38] Jenna Ortiz: Can we get telemetry at token granularity? We need that for some audit requirements.
[06:42] Priya Nair: Yes, we can instrument token-level traces in the Dedicated and Private deployments; for Hosted we provide aggregated token latency histograms and per-request traces on demand. Private gives you full raw traces that you can ship to your logging stack.
[06:56] Marcus Li: Security: SSO, RBAC, KMS?
[07:00] Alex Ramos: We support SAML SSO integrations, fine-grained RBAC, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) for key management. Private deployments can be configured to use your HSM if needed. We'll include the SOC2 docs and our security whitepaper.
[07:14] Samir Patel: One tricky piece — we run summary generation at end of session that sometimes requires 1-2k tokens. How does that affect KV cache and concurrency?
[07:22] Priya Nair: Long-form summaries can be batched differently; they usually increase memory pressure on KV cache and increase per-request compute significantly. We'll model a mixed workload where some sessions trigger long-form jobs. That will affect peak GPU utilization and might push you to a larger Dedicated footprint or offload long-form to separate instance pool.
[07:45] Jenna Ortiz: For cost modeling, do you show cost per active seat or per-token estimates?
[07:50] Alex Ramos: Both. We'll produce a per-token estimate and a per-concurrent-stream cost for your peak windows, plus recommended commit levels for Dedicated.
[07:59] Marcus Li: Timeline — we want a pilot before Q2 end. Is that realistic?
[08:03] Alex Ramos: Yes, pilot within 4-6 weeks is doable: we need your prompt set and a traffic dump, Redwood sets up a Dedicated trial pool for 1-2 weeks, run benchmark, then iterate.
[08:12] Samir Patel: A note on evals — we'll want to compare quality delta if you fallback to smaller quantized models. Does Redwood provide regression tooling?
[08:20] Priya Nair: Redwood Optimize includes regression alerts tied to prompt sets. We'll run the same prompts across variants and capture quality metrics and examples. We'll include that in the benchmark report.
[08:33] Alex Ramos: Anything else on architecture?
[08:35] Jenna Ortiz: Autoscaling cooldowns — we need deterministic behavior during our surge, not oscillation.
[08:40] Priya Nair: We can tune autoscale policies and use pre-warming/burst reservations to avoid oscillation. Dedicated is best when you need deterministic behavior.
[08:48] Marcus Li: Ok, action items?
[08:50] Alex Ramos: I'll send the SOC2 and security docs, Priya will send the benchmark plan, Samir will drop the prompt set. We'll schedule the benchmark run next week.
[08:58] Samir Patel: I'll aim to get the S3 link by Thursday.
[09:00] Jenna Ortiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:03] Alex Ramos: Thanks, we'll follow up with the plan and pricing. Bye.

End of Transcript.
